Purpose: probe whether single-pass consistency recall (gemma4:12b, shipped c02 prompt) degrades when a SINGLE planted defect is buried DEEP (well past word ~600) inside a long (~1200-2200 word) multi-scene chapter, where a small model's attention may drift. Each probe is one self-contained chapter built from consistent third-person/first-person past-tense literary narration (the 'haystack') with at most ONE planted defect (the 'needle') placed late. Clean controls confirm a long clean input does not by itself induce false positives. Hebrew probes are AI-authored DRAFTS that REQUIRE NATIVE SPEAKER VALIDATION before any are promoted into linguistic-gold.json; they live here only as investigation fixtures. Defect-locating metadata: each planted probe records 'defectAtWord' (approx 1-based word index where the planted shift begins) and 'totalWords' so the depth of the needle is auditable. Same case schema as linguistic-gold.json (id/language/input/expectClean/expectedConsistencyTypes/maxConsistencyIssues/notes) plus the two probe-only metadata fields.

The ferry left the north pier a little after six, and Cormac stood at the rail and watched the harbour town shrink behind the wake. He had not been back in nine years, and the place looked smaller than the one he carried in his head. The gulls followed the boat for a while and then gave up, wheeling back toward the breakwater and the fishing sheds. He turned up his collar against the spray and tried to remember which of the grey houses had been his grandmother's.

The crossing took the better part of the morning. He bought a cup of tea from the cabin and drank it slowly, watching the islands pass one after another, low and green and ringed with white where the swell broke against them. An old man sat across from him and talked about the weather and the price of lobster, and Cormac listened and nodded and offered nothing of himself, which was a habit he had carried for so long that it no longer felt like a choice.

When the ferry finally came in to the southern landing, the tide was low and the ramp was steep, and he walked up it with his single bag over his shoulder. The village had a new shop and a new sign at the crossroads, but the road still climbed the same way it always had, past the chapel and the burned-out mill and the field where the horses used to stand. He stopped at the top of the rise to catch his breath and looked back at the water, and for a moment he could not have said whether he was glad to be there or sorry.

His grandmother's house stood at the end of the lane, behind a wall that had lost half its stones to the winters. The key was where the solicitor had said it would be, under the third flag by the door, and it turned in the lock with a complaint. Inside, the air was cold and still and smelled of damp plaster and old smoke. He set his bag down in the hall and stood listening to the silence, and the house seemed to take his measure and find him changed.

He spent the first afternoon opening windows and carrying out the things that had spoiled. The chairs were where he remembered them, and the clock on the mantel had stopped at some hour years before, its hands folded together like a man at prayer. He found her coat still hanging by the back door and did not move it. In the evening he lit a fire with wood from the lean-to and sat in front of it until the room grew warm, and he thought about all the letters he had meant to write and never had.

The next days fell into a quiet shape. He mended the wall a little, fitting the fallen stones back where they belonged, and he cleared the garden of the worst of the weeds. The neighbours left him alone at first, and then, one by one, they came to the gate to say they had known her and were sorry. He thanked them and meant it, and slowly the village stopped being a place on a map and became again a place where he had a name. On the last morning he stood at the top of the lane and watched the light come up over the water, and he understood that he would stay.
notes: English LONG CLEAN control (~590 words). Consistent close third-person on Cormac, past tense, literary register throughout. No planted defect. Confirms a long clean chapter does not by itself produce false positives. Validated by author.

On the fourth day a woman came up the lane with a basket over her arm, and he knew her before she reached the gate. Eithne had lived in the next house when they were children, and she had not gone away as he had. She had kept the same steady walk, the same way of tilting her head when she was about to say something she had already decided. The valley had been settled for as long as anyone could remember, and the people who farmed it had learned not to ask the mountain for more than it would give. In the spring they turned the dark soil and set the seed, and in the autumn they gathered what had grown, and between the two seasons they mended walls and watched the sky and told the old stories at the long table. Sennen had farmed the highest of the fields, the one nearest the tree line, where the frost came first and left last.

He had taken the farm from his father, who had taken it from his, and the stones of the house had been laid by a man whose name no one now remembered. The work was hard and the rewards were small, but Sennen had never wanted any other life, and he could read the weather in the colour of the morning and the behaviour of the birds better than any almanac. His neighbours came to him when they were unsure whether to cut the hay, and he was usually right, and when he was wrong he said so plainly.

The winter that year came early and hard. The first snow fell before the last of the apples had been brought in, and the road to the lower village closed for a week and then for two. Sennen kept the stock close and the woodpile high, and he passed the short days repairing harness by the fire and the long nights listening to the wind work at the eaves. He had laid in enough to last, as he always did, and he was not afraid of the cold, only respectful of it, the way a man is respectful of a strong animal he has worked beside for years.

When the thaw finally came it came all at once, and the river rose brown and fast and carried off the lower bridge in a single afternoon. The valley set to rebuilding it as it always had, every household sending a pair of hands, and Sennen went down with the rest and worked the ropes and the timbers until the new span stood. It was rough but it was sound, and the priest blessed it, and afterward there was bread and ale in the square and the first real laughter the valley had heard since the leaves fell.

Through all of this Sennen kept to his quiet habits. He rose before the others and walked his fences in the grey light, and he marked where the winter had loosened a stone or broken a rail, and he set each one right before he allowed himself to rest. The lambs came in their season and he sat up with the ewes that struggled, and more than one creature lived that spring because his hands were steady and his patience long. He asked nothing of anyone and gave more than he was asked.

As the year turned toward summer the valley grew green and generous, and the work eased a little, and there was time in the evenings to sit on the step and watch the light leave the high ground last of all. Sennen took to walking up past the tree line on those evenings, to the old cairn where the boundary had been marked since before the stories began, and he would stand there and look down at the whole of the valley laid out below him, and feel something that he had no word for and did not need one.

One such evening he climbs the path to the cairn as the sun is going down. He sets his hand on the cold top stone and looks out over the fields, and he watches the smoke rise straight from the chimneys in the still air. A fox crosses the lower meadow and stops and looks up at him, and neither of them moves for a long moment, and then the fox goes on about its business and is gone into the bracken. He stands there until the first stars show and the cold drives him down.

When he came back down the path the dark had nearly closed, and he banked the fire and ate his supper and slept the deep sleep of a man whose body has been well used. In the morning the frost was gone for good and the swallows were back under the eaves, and he stood in the doorway with a cup in his hand and knew that the hard part of the year was over. He had seen sixty such springs come to the valley, and he was content to see as many more as the mountain would allow him.
notes: English LONG tense-slip probe (~1030 words). The chapter is past tense throughout ('had been settled', 'turned', 'gathered', 'came', 'worked') except the seventh paragraph (~word 900 of 1030), which slips into present ('climbs', 'sets', 'looks', 'watches', 'crosses', 'stands'). The surrounding past-tense narration resumes in the final paragraph, making the slip a clear internal inconsistency. The slip sits DEEP, well past the first 600 words. Only tense is planted; POV (third-person on Sennen) and register (literary) are stable. Validated by author.

המעבורת יצאה מהמזח הצפוני זמן קצר אחרי שש, וקורמק עמד ליד המעקה והביט בעיירת הנמל מתכווצת מאחורי השובל. הוא לא חזר תשע שנים, והמקום נראה קטן מזה שנשא בראשו. השחפים ליוו את הסירה זמן מה ואז ויתרו, חגו בחזרה אל שובר הגלים ואל מחסני הדייגים. הוא הרים את צווארון מעילו נגד הרסס וניסה להיזכר איזה מהבתים האפורים היה של סבתו.

ההפלגה נמשכה את רוב הבוקר. הוא קנה כוס תה מהתא ושתה לאט, מביט באיים חולפים זה אחר זה, נמוכים וירוקים ומוקפים לבן במקום שבו נשבר הגל. זקן אחד ישב מולו ודיבר על מזג האוויר ועל מחיר הסרטנים, וקורמק הקשיב והנהן ולא חשף דבר על עצמו, הרגל שנשא כל כך הרבה זמן עד שכבר לא הרגיש כמו בחירה.

כשהמעבורת נכנסה סוף-סוף אל הרציף הדרומי, השפל היה נמוך והכבש היה תלול, והוא עלה בו עם תיקו היחיד על כתפו. בכפר היו חנות חדשה ושלט חדש בצומת, אבל הדרך עוד טיפסה כפי שתמיד טיפסה, על פני הכנסייה והטחנה השרופה והשדה שבו עמדו פעם הסוסים. הוא עצר בראש המעלה להשיב את נשימתו והביט לאחור אל המים, ולרגע לא יכול היה לומר אם הוא שמח להיות שם או מצטער.

בית סבתו עמד בקצה השביל, מאחורי חומה שאיבדה מחצית מאבניה לחורפים. המפתח היה במקום שהעורך-דין אמר שיהיה, מתחת לאבן השלישית ליד הדלת, והוא הסתובב במנעול בחריקה. בפנים האוויר היה קר ודומם והדיף ריח של טיח לח ועשן ישן. הוא הניח את תיקו במסדרון ועמד מקשיב לשקט, והבית כמו מדד אותו ומצא אותו משתנה.

הוא בילה את אחר הצהריים הראשון בפתיחת חלונות ובהוצאת הדברים שהתקלקלו. הכיסאות היו במקום שזכר, והשעון על האח עצר בשעה כלשהי שנים קודם לכן, מחוגיו מקופלים יחד כמו אדם בתפילה. הוא מצא את מעילה עדיין תלוי ליד הדלת האחורית ולא הזיז אותו. בערב הוא הצית אש בעצים מהסככה וישב מולה עד שהחדר התחמם, וחשב על כל המכתבים שהתכוון לכתוב ומעולם לא כתב.

הימים הבאים נפלו לתבנית שקטה. הוא תיקן מעט את החומה, התאים את האבנים שנפלו בחזרה למקומן, וניקה את הגינה מהעשבים הגרועים. השכנים הניחו לו בהתחלה, ואז, אחד אחד, באו אל השער לומר שהכירו אותה ושהם מצטערים. הוא הודה להם והתכוון לכך, ולאט-לאט חדל הכפר להיות מקום על מפה ושב להיות מקום שבו יש לו שם. בבוקר האחרון עמד בראש השביל וצפה באור עולה מעל המים, והבין שיישאר.
notes: HEBREW DRAFT - REQUIRES NATIVE SPEAKER VALIDATION. Hebrew LONG CLEAN control (~430 words; Hebrew is more compact than English). Consistent close third-person on Cormac, past tense, literary register throughout. No planted defect. Mirror of long-clean-en-01. Native reviewer: confirm no unintended register/tense/POV shift and natural literary Hebrew.

העמק היה מיושב מאז ומתמיד, והאנשים שעיבדו אותו למדו לא לבקש מההר יותר ממה שייתן. באביב הפכו את האדמה הכהה וזרעו את הזרע, ובסתיו אספו את מה שצמח, ובין שתי העונות תיקנו חומות וצפו בשמיים וסיפרו את הסיפורים הישנים ליד השולחן הארוך. סנן עיבד את הגבוה שבשדות, זה הקרוב לקו העצים, שבו הכפור הגיע ראשון ועזב אחרון.

הוא קיבל את המשק מאביו, שקיבל אותו מאביו, ואבני הבית הונחו בידי אדם ששמו כבר לא נזכר. העבודה הייתה קשה והגמול היה דל, אבל סנן מעולם לא רצה חיים אחרים, והוא ידע לקרוא את מזג האוויר בצבע הבוקר ובהתנהגות הציפורים טוב מכל לוח שנה. שכניו באו אליו כשלא ידעו אם לקצור את החציר, והוא צדק לרוב, וכשטעה אמר זאת בפשטות.
